passage_text: Researchers studied the effects of three different cognitive training programs on working memory performance in adults aged 25–35. A total of 120 participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group (no training) and three experimental groups that received either a visuospatial training program (Group V), a verbal training program (Group W), or a combined visuospatial–verbal program (Group C). Each training program consisted of 30‑minute sessions, three times per week, over eight weeks. Working memory was assessed before and after the intervention using the Digit Span and Corsi Block‑Tapping tasks. Table 1 summarizes the mean post‑intervention scores and standard deviations for each group. The researchers hypothesized that the combined program would yield the greatest improvement, followed by the visuospatial and verbal programs, with the control group showing minimal change. The results indicated that Group C achieved the highest mean score, while Group V and Group W performed similarly, and the control group had the lowest scores.
stem: Which group had the highest mean post‑intervention working memory score?
explanation: Table 1 shows the Combined (C) group with a mean score of 60.3, the highest among all groups.
trap: Choosing the visuospatial group because it comes first among the trained groups; the combined group's 60.3 is the highest mean.

stem: Which study design best describes the researchers’ methodology?
explanation: Participants were randomly assigned to groups and received specific interventions, which is characteristic of a randomized controlled trial.
trap: Choosing a cross-sectional design; random assignment to interventions followed by re-testing defines a randomized controlled trial.

stem: Table 1 reports only post‑intervention means and SDs. Which of the following cannot be determined from Table 1 alone?

options.A: How much each group's working memory score changed from before to after training
options.B: Which group had the highest post‑intervention mean
options.C: The difference in post‑intervention means between Group C and Group V
options.D: Whether the control group's post‑intervention mean was lower than every trained group's

explanation: Correct: Change from baseline needs pre-intervention scores, which Table 1 does not give. Why the others are wrong: B) Group C's 60.3 is the highest listed mean. C) 60.3 − 53.7 = 6.6 is computed directly from the table. D) The control mean, 45.2, is below 52.9, 53.7 and 60.3.
trap: Assuming the improvement in each group can be read from the table, when only the final scores are shown.

stem: Which observation in Table 1 best supports the hypothesis that the combined program outperformed the single-modality programs?

options.A: Group C's mean (60.3) exceeded both Group V's (53.7) and Group W's (52.9)
options.B: Group V's mean (53.7) was slightly higher than Group W's (52.9)
options.C: The control group's SD (5.1) was the largest
options.D: Every trained group scored higher than the control group

explanation: Correct: Only a higher mean for the combined group than for each single-modality group addresses the comparison in the hypothesis (60.3 versus 53.7 and 52.9). Why the others are wrong: B) the V versus W comparison says nothing about the combined program. C) a group's SD describes variability, not which program works best. D) all trained groups beating control (45.2) shows training helps but does not show combined is better than single-modality programs.
trap: Treating 'all trained groups beat control' as evidence that the combined program is best.
